title: More Correct Mass, Worse Answers: Where Power Sampling Breaks
hook: Sharpening a model's distribution can push more probability onto correct reasoning paths and still make the final answer worse — by up to 18.5 points. The culprit is coverage, not correctness.
key_points: Power Sampling sharpens the distribution over whole generation trajectories — a verifier-free reasoning boost.
Paradox: it can raise probability mass on correct trajectories while degrading downstream self-consistency.
Reported accuracy drops of up to 18.5 percentage points across models and reasoning benchmarks.
Dose mismatch: one fixed exponent causes wildly different amounts of sharpening per problem.
Coverage mismatch: global sharpening concentrates mass on a few dominant paths, so high pass@k can hide lost path diversity.
Fix: a deformation-controlled, support-preserving target that limits suppression of moderate-probability paths.
content_html: Power Sampling is a verifier-free way to improve reasoning at inference time: sharpen the model's distribution over complete generation trajectories so that better paths get more mass. It's attractive as a general front end for other sampling methods. This paper finds it can backfire — pushing more probability onto correct trajectories while making the downstream answer worse, with accuracy drops of up to 18.5 percentage points when self-consistency sits on top.
extra_html:
Two mismatches

Dose mismatch. A single fixed exponent doesn't mean the same thing to every problem's distribution — it induces drastically different amounts of distributional change depending on the problem, over-sharpening some and barely touching others.

Coverage mismatch. Global sharpening concentrates mass onto a narrow set of dominant paths. That's fatal for anything that aggregates: self-consistency, search, and selection all need broad support over reasoning paths, not just a peak. The subtle part is that pass@k stays high — usually read as proof that diversity survived — even as the support that downstream aggregation depends on collapses.

The repair

The authors replace uniform trajectory exponentiation with a deformation-controlled, support-preserving Power target: calibrate the amount of sharpening per problem, and cap how much moderate-probability paths get suppressed. Instantiated with weighted self-consistency at the same budget, the repaired sampler recovers the losses. The transferable lesson is that "the distribution got better" is not the same claim as "the pipeline that consumes the distribution got better."

related.hook: Sample the model many times, let each run reason its own way, then take the majority answer - diverse reasoning paths vote out individual errors.

related.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute
related.hook: A new scaling axis: instead of a bigger model, let a model think longer at inference — often a better use of compute, and the principle behind o1 and R1.

related.title: Refute, Don't Resample: Claim-Level Reliability Assessment
related.hook: Refuting a wrong claim needs one decisive flaw; building a right answer needs a flawless path. CLR spends test-time compute on that asymmetry instead of on more samples.

related.title: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
related.hook: Sample a reasoning model dozens of times and coverage keeps climbing — but picking the right answer from the pile plateaus fast, and extra samples past that point can backfire.

flashcards.prompt: How can Power Sampling put more mass on correct trajectories yet lower final accuracy?
flashcards.back_html: Downstream methods like self-consistency need broad support across reasoning paths. Global sharpening concentrates mass on a few dominant paths, so aggregation has less to work with even though correct mass rose.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'dose mismatch' in this paper?

choices.text: A fixed sharpening exponent induces drastically different amounts of distributional change across problems
The sampler uses the wrong temperature for the model's size
Too many samples are drawn per problem relative to the budget

flashcards.explanation_html: Dose mismatch is the problem that one fixed exponent over-sharpens some problems and barely touches others, because the same exponent means different things to different distributions.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a high pass@k misleading here?

choices.text: It can coexist with the loss of the broad path support that aggregation and search need
It is measured on a different benchmark than self-consistency
It always falls when sharpening increases

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper notes high pass@k is often read as evidence of preserved diversity, but it can hold even as the broad reasoning-path support required for downstream aggregation, search, and selection disappears.
